newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition mulls watered-down tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: German coalition mulls watered-down tax reforms.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government may scale back its tax reforms in a bid to win over a defiant opposition, German coalition sources said on Friday.

The sources confirmed media reports that the government was considering lopping 15 billion marks ($8 billion) off Germans' tax bills in 1998 -- half the sum originally planned by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
To help to pay for direct tax cuts next year, the 15 percent rate of value-added tax would rise by one point. A further one-point rise is already planned to pay for pensions reforms.

Kohl and Waigel want to push through the tax reforms at the second attempt after their original plan was blocked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in parliament's upper house and later in the legislative mediation committee.
But, although the SPD has signalled its willingness to talk again on tax, it objects to VAT hikes to pay for the reforms.
"We will not agree to any increase in VAT through which consumers will pay for tax gifts to millionaires," SPD chief whip Peter Struck said.

Struck, speaking to the Magdeburger Volksstimme newspaper, said he held out little hope of reaching a deal on tax. The two sides have held a sputtering series of talks stretching back to last winter, but have failed to make progress.
"I wouldn't bet on reaching a deal," Struck said, adding that the SPD would do better to introduce its own tax reform if it won general elections in September 1998.
Finance Ministry sources said the government had not yet worked out a comprehensive new tax position.

But ideas being aired by some coalition leaders indicate the government is prepared to go some way towards easing fears in the SPD that Waigel's original reform would rip a huge hole in state finances.

Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), said on Thursday that top-rate income tax could be cut to 45 percent next year from 53 percent, instead of an initial proposal of 39 percent.
The main rate of corporation tax could fall from 47 percent to 40 percent, instead of the 35 percent earlier envisaged by the coalition.
Coalition sources said the bottom rate of income tax could also fall to just over 20 percent from 25.9 percent now.

Total direct tax cuts could be between 50 and 60 billion marks. That would be offset by 15 billion marks from the VAT hike and the scrapping of between 20 and 30 billion marks in tax breaks, leaving net tax cuts of 15 billion marks.
The coalition and SPD informally agreed in the first round of parliamentary mediation on a list of tax exemptions to abolish.
But the two sides are still far apart on where new tax rates should be set. The government has also refused to bow to SPD demands to raise tax-free allowances and child benefits.
The SPD wants the government to back cuts in unemployment insurance contributions -- but that would require an increase in petrol taxes on top of the higher VAT.
